title: Personal protective equipment
blurb: Choose PPE by assessing the exposure risk, and put it on and take it off in the right order.
question: A nurse is about to irrigate a large infected leg wound and expects fluid to splash towards her face. No full-face visor is available. Which facial protection should she wear?

teach.h: PPE is chosen by risk, not by habit
teach.body: Before any task, assess the likely exposure to blood, body fluids, non-intact skin or mucous membranes, then wear PPE that protects adequately against that risk. The NIPCM stresses that avoiding overuse is a key principle: unnecessary PPE wastes resources, harms the environment and, in the case of gloves, can increase infection risk. Put simply: no exposure expected, no PPE needed; contact expected, gloves and apron; splash expected, add face protection.

head: Expected exposure
Gloves
Apron
FRSM + eye
rows: None to blood, body fluid, mucosa or broken skin
Exposure, but no splash or spray
teach.caption: Hand hygiene before putting on and after removing PPE. PPE is removed in the patient care area, apart from FFP3 respirators and eye protection when there is no anteroom.

rows.label: Routine IM, SC or intradermal injections

teach.note: Change gloves after each task (even on the same patient), after touching surroundings, if damaged, and before leaving the bed space. Never wash or handrub gloves.

teach.body: A fluid-resistant surgical mask (Type IIR) protects the wearer's nose and mouth from splashes, and is worn with eye protection when no full-face visor is available. A Type II or IIR mask protects the patient from the operator during procedures such as central line insertion. An FRSM is also part of droplet precautions within 1 metre. An FFP3 respirator protects the wearer from aerosols: it is considered for airborne pathogens and for aerosol generating procedures (AGPs) on patients with a respiratory infection.

rows.label: Fit test
values: Fit test before use, fit check every time

rows.label: Worn by patient?
values: No, never by an infectious patient

teach.caption: Facial hair must not cross the respirator seal. If a fit cannot be achieved, a powered respirator hood is the alternative.

With no anteroom, FFP3 respirators and eye protection are removed in a safe area outside the room; other PPE is removed in the patient area. Perform hand hygiene between steps as local policy requires and always at the end.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Tomasz and Mrs Hill
teach.body: Tomasz is irrigating Mrs Hill's infected leg ulcer and splashing towards his face is likely. No visor is available, so he wears a Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with separate eye protection, plus an apron and non-sterile gloves. His prescription glasses are not eye protection. Afterwards he removes gloves, apron, eye protection, then mask, and decontaminates his hands. For her routine medicines later that day he needs no PPE at all.

teach.text: Two classic confusions. First, prescription glasses are NOT eye protection. Second, an FFP3 respirator protects the wearer from incoming air; it must never be put on an infectious patient, who wears an FRSM as source control instead.

items: Assess exposure first; avoid PPE overuse, especially gloves.
No gloves for oral medicines, routine injections, observations, mobilising or comforting.
Sterile gloves for sterile sites and aseptic procedures such as urinary catheter insertion.
Type IIR FRSM plus eye protection for splash risk; FFP3 (fit tested and fit checked) for airborne risks and AGPs.
On: apron, mask, eyes, gloves. Off: gloves, apron, eyes, mask, then hand hygiene.

summary: You can now select PPE by assessing the expected exposure, tell an FRSM from an FFP3 respirator and know when each is used. You can also put PPE on and take it off in the order that limits self-contamination.

A.q: Mr Ahmed, 64, needs his routine subcutaneous enoxaparin. His skin is intact and he has no known infection. Which PPE does the nurse need?
options: Non-sterile gloves and an apron
Non-sterile gloves
Sterile gloves and an apron
No PPE; hand hygiene is enough
A.why: The NIPCM lists routine intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular injections among tasks where gloves are not routinely worn, as no blood or body fluid exposure is anticipated.

whyNot.0: No contamination of the uniform is expected, so neither apron nor gloves are indicated.
whyNot.1: Gloves are not routinely needed for routine SC injections and their overuse is discouraged.
whyNot.2: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures, not routine injections.

A.q: Which procedure requires sterile gloves under the NIPCM?
options: Inserting a urinary catheter
Emptying a urinary drainage bag
Giving a bed bath
Removing a peripheral cannula
A.why: Sterile gloves are required to preserve a sterile field during aseptic procedures, and the NIPCM gives urinary catheter insertion as an example.

whyNot.1: Emptying a bag involves possible body fluid exposure but not a sterile site: non-sterile gloves.
whyNot.2: A bed bath may need non-sterile gloves for contact with body fluids but no sterile field.
whyNot.3: Cannula removal needs non-sterile gloves because blood exposure is possible, not a sterile field.

A.q: A nurse has finished caring for Mrs Ward, who has influenza, and is wearing gloves, an apron, goggles and an FRSM. In which order should she remove them?
options: Gloves, apron, eye protection, then mask
Mask, eye protection, apron, and then gloves
Apron, gloves, mask, then eye protection
Eye protection, mask, gloves, then apron
A.why: Doffing starts with the most contaminated item (gloves), then apron or gown, then eye protection, and the mask last, followed by hand hygiene (NIPCM appendix 6).

whyNot.1: Removing the mask first means touching the face with contaminated gloves.
whyNot.2: The apron is removed after the gloves, and the mask comes off last.
whyNot.3: Touching the eyes and face first with gloved hands risks self-contamination.

B.q: Nurse Femi is irrigating a heavily infected wound and splashing towards his face is likely. No full-face visor is available. Which facial protection should he wear?
options: His prescription glasses with a Type IIR mask
A Type IIR FRSM with separate eye protection
An FFP3 respirator with no eye protection
A Type II surgical mask with no eye protection
B.why: Where a visor is unavailable and splashing onto the nose and mouth is likely, a Type IIR FRSM is worn with eye protection (NIPCM 1.4).

whyNot.0: Regular corrective spectacles are not considered eye protection.
whyNot.2: FFP3 is for airborne risks and AGPs; it does not protect the eyes from splashes.
whyNot.3: Type II masks are not fluid resistant, and the eyes would be unprotected.

B.q: Daniel has a full beard and must care for a patient with suspected measles in a negative-pressure room. He passed a fit test months ago when clean-shaven. What should he wear?
options: A tight-fitting FFP3 respirator with a careful fit check
A Type IIR FRSM with eye protection
A powered respirator hood in place of the FFP3
Two FRSMs worn one over the other
B.why: Facial hair must not cross the respirator seal, so a tight-fitting FFP3 will not seal. Powered respirator hoods are the alternative when a fit cannot be achieved (NIPCM 2.4).

whyNot.0: A fit check cannot overcome a beard crossing the seal; the old fit test no longer applies.
whyNot.1: An FRSM does not protect against airborne measles; respiratory protection is needed.
whyNot.3: Doubling FRSMs does not create a respirator seal or filter aerosols.

B.q: Mr Brennan, who has suspected influenza, needs to go to the X-ray department through a busy corridor. Which protection is most appropriate for him during the transfer?
options: An FFP3 respirator, if he can tolerate wearing one
A cloth face covering from home
No mask, as the escorting staff will wear FFP3 respirators
A fluid-resistant surgical mask if he can tolerate it
B.why: Infectious patients transferred through communal areas should wear an FRSM as source control if tolerated and safe (NIPCM 2.1 and 2.4).

whyNot.0: FFP3 respirators filter incoming air and must never be worn by an infectious patient.
whyNot.1: Healthcare source control uses an FRSM, not a cloth covering.
whyNot.2: Source control on the patient is advised; escort staff in FFP3 does not protect others in the corridor.

C.q: Nurse Ama wears gloves and an apron to empty Mr Kowalski's stoma bag. She now needs to give him mouth care at the same bedside. What should she do first?
options: Wipe the gloves with handrub and continue
Keep the same gloves on, as it is one patient
Remove the gloves, decontaminate hands, put on new gloves
Put a second pair of gloves on over the first pair for mouth care
C.why: Gloves are changed after completing a task even on the same patient, with hand hygiene between glove changes (NIPCM 1.4).

whyNot.0: Gloves must never be decontaminated with handrub or soap between uses.
whyNot.1: Organisms from the stoma would be carried to the mouth; gloves are changed between tasks.
whyNot.3: Double gloving is not recommended for routine care and does not replace a change.

C.q: A healthcare assistant is about to take routine observations on six patients in a bay, none with known infection. She puts on gloves 'to be safe'. What is the best advice?
options: Keep the gloves on but change them between each patient
Remove them; gloves are not needed for observations
Add an apron as well for full protection
Wear one pair for the bay, then discard them
C.why: Taking observations involves no anticipated exposure to blood or body fluids, so gloves are not routinely worn. Glove overuse increases cross-infection risk and does not replace hand hygiene (NIPCM 1.4).

whyNot.0: Changing between patients is right when gloves are needed, but here they are not indicated.
whyNot.2: No contamination of clothing is anticipated, so an apron adds nothing.
whyNot.3: Using one pair across patients would carry organisms around the bay.

C.q: A nurse leaves an isolation room with no anteroom after caring for a patient with tuberculosis. She wore an apron, gloves, an FFP3 respirator and goggles. Where should she remove the respirator and goggles?
options: Inside the room, before the apron and gloves
Inside the room, after the apron and gloves
At the nurses' station once her notes have been written
In a safe area outside the room, after leaving
C.why: Without an anteroom, FFP3 respirators and eye or face protection are removed in a safe area outside the isolation room; other PPE is removed in the patient area (NIPCM 2.4).

whyNot.0: Gloves come off before facial protection, and the respirator stays on while still in the room's air.
whyNot.1: Removing the respirator inside the room exposes her to aerosols still in the air.
whyNot.2: PPE should be removed in a designated safe area promptly, not worn into general areas such as the nurses' station.

reteach.title: Match the barrier to the route
reteach.question: Ask yourself: what could reach me, and where would it land?

blocks.body: Will my hands touch blood or body fluid? Gloves. Will my uniform get contaminated? Apron (gown if splashing is extensive). Could something splash or travel to my face? Eye protection and an FRSM, or an FFP3 respirator if the threat is airborne. If the answer to all three is no, you need hand hygiene and nothing else.

blocks.text: On: apron, mask, eyes, gloves. Off: gloves, apron, eyes, mask. Gloves go on last and come off first.

explain.body: Gloves when exposure to blood, body fluids (including saliva), broken skin or mucous membranes is anticipated. Not for oral medicines, routine injections, observations, mobilising, comforting or paperwork.

test.q: For which task should a nurse wear non-sterile gloves?
options: Giving a patient oral tablets
Taking a blood pressure
Giving mouth care
Helping a patient to walk
test.why: Mouth care involves contact with saliva and mucous membranes, so non-sterile gloves are indicated.

whyNot.0: Oral medicine administration is listed as not routinely needing gloves.
whyNot.1: Taking observations involves no expected exposure to body fluids.
whyNot.3: Mobilising a patient is listed as a task where gloves are not routinely worn.

explain.body: A single-use apron when contamination of uniform is anticipated, changed between patients and after each task. A full gown or fluid-resistant coverall when splashing is extensive or an apron gives inadequate cover.

test.q: When should a disposable apron be changed?
options: Between patients and after each task
At the end of each drug round
When it becomes visibly soiled or damaged
Every hour during a shift
test.why: Aprons are single use and changed between patients and after completing a procedure or task (NIPCM 1.4).

whyNot.1: An apron worn across a round carries organisms between patients.
whyNot.2: Contamination is often invisible, so waiting for soiling is too late.
whyNot.3: Changes are linked to patients and tasks, not to time.

explain.body: Type IIR FRSM: splash protection (with eye protection) and droplet precautions within 1 metre; also patient source control. FFP3: airborne pathogens and AGPs, fit tested and fit checked each time, never worn by an infectious patient.

head: Situation
Mask
rows: Patient with cough in a bay

test.q: What must a nurse do every time she puts on an FFP3 respirator?
options: Arrange a new fit test
Perform a fit check
Wear it under an FRSM
Moisten the seal with water
test.why: A fit test is done in advance; a fit check is performed every time the respirator is donned to confirm the seal (NIPCM 2.4).

whyNot.0: Fit testing is done before first use, not at every donning.
whyNot.2: An FRSM is not layered with an FFP3 as standard practice.
whyNot.3: Moistening the seal is not part of manufacturers' fit checking.

explain.body: Donning: hand hygiene, apron or gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves. Doffing: gloves, apron or gown, eye protection, mask or respirator, hand hygiene.

test.q: Which item of PPE is put on last?
options: The apron
The FRSM
Eye protection
Gloves
test.why: Gloves go on last so that they are clean for the task and do not touch the mask or eyewear during donning.

whyNot.0: The apron or gown goes on first after hand hygiene.
whyNot.1: The mask goes on second, before eye protection.
whyNot.2: Eye protection goes on before gloves.
